newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Economists share RBNZ concern on current account.
newsitem.headline: Economists share RBNZ concern on current account.

text.p: Economists on Thursday warned a worsening New Zealand current account could in time see a sharp fall in the currency and a rise in interest rates.

The Reserve Bank, in its six-monthly economic projections, saw the balance of payments deficit reaching NZ$6.2 billion in the year to March 1999, or 5.9 percent of nominal GDP. In September it had forecast the deficit to peak at $4 billion in 1998, or 4.2 percent of GDP.
It said a deficit of this size was unlikely to be sustained indefinitely and would be corrected by either a rise in savings or substantial capital outflows.
Economists contacted by Reuters shared the bank's view and warned of the dangers of a sudden "rebalancing" of the currency and interest rates.

"As we head towards six percent (of GDP) and go through that, it will become a focal point and credit rating agencies will draw attention to it more and more," Deutsche Bank economist Ulf Schoefisch said.
Garlick and Co economist Matthew Goodson said the current account deficit was not a problem if it could be financed.

"But when you have got 62 percent of your bond market owned offshore and about the same in your equity market, you have to question whether those capital inflows are one-time portfolio allocations or whether they are going to continue ad infinitum."

Integrated Economic Services economist Petrus Simons said: "If overseas investors see...the level of the deficit is six percent, you get close to a position where they are likely to withdraw their money and so start a selloff triggering a depreciation of the exchange rate."
The economists agreed a deficit was acceptable if it was spent on investments which produce exports.
"But I would suggest some of our investment goods have not been applied in that fashion, so I don't think you can apply that argument to New Zealand," Goodson said.
"I think consumption will play a pretty strong role here. The structure of the economy that is going to evolve over the next few years is in my view not a very healthy one," said Schoefisch.

He said New Zealand had in the past congratulated itself on a market-led growth with no artificial government stimulus, but extra government spending would change that. The centre-right coalition plans $5 billion extra spending over three years.
Opposition finance spokesman Michael Cullen said the deficit projections were a sign of huge imbalances in the economy.

"The projections show us going over the line where there is usually concern, at about five percent, and the economy is only growing at 2.5 percent on average. That starts to raise concerns about the ability to service that level of indebtedness," he said in a telephone interview.

"I think the government needs to get a correction of the dollar very quickly now. It can't avoid an inflationary consequence of an adjustment. But at least if it can engineer a modest reduction now with an impact on the current account then there is a real chance that we don't get a crunch further down the track," Cullen said, agreeing that that could see the dollar dive and interest rates soar.
Goodson said if the deficit became a problem, the bank would have difficulty controlling the monetary policy mix.
"They could get a rebalancing in a real hurry between the exchange rate and interest rates," Goodson said.
"That is the Armageddon scenario. There is only a very small probability of a nasty outcome, but a small probability times a large move equals a little bit that has to be built in."

While Schoefisch shared the concerns of the bank and other economists, he said the make-up of the deficit should be taken into account. A significant portion was retained earnings of foreign companies, and half of that was reinvested in New Zealand. -- Wellington newsroom 64 4 4734 746
